conversation.content:
Hello—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician who works specifically with new mothers. Over the next few minutes I’d like to do a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s a short, 10-question tool that helps us see how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, so we can make sure you’re getting any support you might need. Everything you share stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words; I’ll jot down the information. Ready to start?

First question: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[slow exhale]  
Lately… most things don’t feel very funny. I’ll see a silly meme or hear my husband joking with the baby and I know I “should” laugh, but it lands flat—like I’m watching it through thick glass. I might force a little chuckle so no one worries, but genuine laughter? That hasn’t really happened this week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]  
That doesn’t feel true for me right now. I mean, I can manage a polite little laugh if someone else is laughing, but it’s not the same—it’s not coming from inside me. Things that used to crack me up just feel kind of dull or exhausting.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet for a second]  
Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it feels like I’m just getting through the day. When I think about plans, my stomach kind of sinks instead of fluttering.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that one hits. If the baby won’t settle or I can’t figure out why he’s crying, my brain jumps straight to “I’m failing at this.” Even silly stuff—like forgetting to switch the laundry—turns into “I’m a terrible mom, I can’t handle anything.” I know it’s probably not fair, but I still feel it almost every day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands in lap]  
Pretty much all the time. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly think, “What if he stops breathing?” or I’ll hear a siren and picture horrible accidents. There’s no real reason—he’s healthy, the doctors say everything’s fine—but the thoughts just crash in and I can’t settle them for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like this sudden wave—my heart races, I feel shaky, and I have to check on the baby again even though I just did. It passes after a few minutes, but it keeps happening, especially at night when the house is quiet.
Things have been getting on top of me

[eyes fill]  
Yes. Most of the day feels like I’m drowning in small tasks—diapers, bottles, texts I haven’t answered, laundry mountain. I’ll sit to rest and my mind keeps spinning with everything I still “should” do. Some afternoons I just stare at the wall while he naps because I don’t know where to start.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[nods slowly]  
That’s been happening a lot. I’ll finally get him down, crawl into bed myself, and then my brain won’t shut off—rerunning every little thing I think I did wrong, worrying about tomorrow. Some nights I’m awake until two or three, even though I’m exhausted.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard]  
Yeah… most of the week I’ve felt heavy and weepy. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be holding the baby and tears just start rolling. I keep thinking I should be happy—he’s here, he’s healthy—but the sadness sticks around.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[eyes well up again]  
Yes… it’s happened a few times just since the weekend. Yesterday I cried while folding his tiny onesies because I felt like I wasn’t doing enough, even though the basket was empty. The tears come out of nowhere and then I feel guilty for wasting time crying when I could be sleeping or cleaning.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and cried, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of my son.

You've shared how the joy and spark that used to come easily now feel distant; days are clouded by heavy <sym>sadness</sym>, constant <sym>worry</sym>, and a sense of drowning in everyday tasks. Despite your deep love for your baby, you feel stuck in self-doubt, cry often, and lie awake trapped by racing thoughts, yet you bravely state you have no wish to harm yourself and simply want to feel better.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes complete loss of spontaneous laughter and finds previously amusing things dull/exhausting, aligning with 'Not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a near-complete loss of anticipatory joy, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "almost every day" for both major and minor incidents, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes episodic panic-like symptoms that occur repeatedly, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most of the day," unable to manage even small tasks, and mentally paralyzed—clearly matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent insomnia driven by persistent negative thoughts, aligning with 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness, frequent crying, and persistent low mood matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes several crying episodes in just a few days, triggered by feelings of inadequacy, which aligns with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 on the EPDS places you well above the ≥14 cutoff denoting probable major <med>depressive episode</med> with peripartum onset. You describe nearly complete loss of enjoyment (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), daily crying, disproportionate guilt, and multiple <sym>somatic</sym> and <sym>cognitive symptoms</sym> present "most of the time," consistent with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for Major Depressive Disorder. Your endorsement of <sym>panic-like symptoms</sym> and constant <sym>rumination</sym> also suggests co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>PCP</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med>
2. Ask about starting evidenced-based <med>therapy</med> (CBT or interpersonal therapy) and discuss possible <med>antidepressant</med> options compatible with breastfeeding
3. Plan practical daytime support: enlist family/friends for baby care, meals, or household tasks to allow rest
4. Prioritise <sym>sleep hygiene</sym>: brief afternoon rest when baby naps, low lights and no screens after night feeds
5. Follow up with formal counselling on <sym>self-blame</sym> and <sym>parenting confidence</sym>; local <med>support groups</med> or online communities can reduce isolation
6. Schedule EPDS re-screen in 2 weeks to monitor progress and adjust supports as needed
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]  
Clinician: [name], LCSW  
Source: Patient self-report, 10-item Edinburgh Plus Anxiety items (charted verbatim)

Symptoms / Concerns  
- Marked anhedonia (Q1, Q2)  
- Pervasive dysphoria with daily crying spells (Q8, Q9)  
- Sleep-onset insomnia linked to ruminative guilt (Q7)  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt re parenting performance (Q3)  
- Recurrent intrusive “what-if” fears & nocturnal panic episodes (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed / “drowning” (Q6)

Pattern  
Consistent low mood, loss of pleasure, heightened anxiety, and functional overload beginning post-delivery; symptoms present “most days” and “most of the week.”

Screening Significance  
Meets threshold indicators for possible Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and co-occurring anxiety symptoms; level of distress moderate-severe, coping compromised.

Safety  
Denies any self-harm ideation (Q10); no suicidal intent or plan elicited. Continue routine safety monitoring.

Next Steps  
Schedule follow-up within one week for standardized EPDS, differential screening (thyroid, anemia), psychoeducation, and discussion of supports / treatment options.
